claims.text: The untreated alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle failure.
Dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries create local stress concentrations that cause microcracking and brittle failure.
A single additional aging treatment can induce coherent nanoprecipitates in the alloy.
The aging-induced nanoprecipitates will be uniformly distributed throughout the lamellar structure.
The proposed precipitates are analogous to the coherent δ-lamellae and γ″ particles produced by stepwise thermo-mechanical processing in the cited refractory alloy.
The coherent nanoprecipitates will form at or near internal lamellar boundaries.
The coherent nanoprecipitates will facilitate dislocation transmission across lamellar boundaries by allowing dislocations to shear through the precipitates.
Precipitate-assisted dislocation transmission will relieve stress concentrations at lamellar boundaries and mitigate dislocation pile-ups.
Relieving boundary stress concentrations will decrease local microcracking and catastrophic damage.
The precipitates will provide additional strengthening through lattice-misfit and order hardening.
The aged alloy will have greater tensile ductility than the untreated alloy at room temperature.
The aged alloy will retain or exceed the tensile strength of the untreated alloy.
Room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate near 5 × 10^-4 s^-1 is an applicable evaluation condition.
TEM and EBSD can be used to characterize the processed microstructure.
The intervention is applicable across eutectic high-entropy alloys with hierarchical lamellar colonies when pile-up-induced cracking is the primary limitation.
The quantitative strength and ductility gains depend on precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution.
Optimal aging temperature and duration must be tailored to the particular alloy system.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows strength merely to be retained while ductility improves, but the falsification rule says no improvement in strength and/or ductility is sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. Thus, unchanged strength could be treated as falsifying even though it is explicitly permitted by the predicted outcome.
